# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

If you'd rather skip the questions and have me start building, just say so.

**What hasn't happened**

# Metadata Budget v1 (Pilot)

## Normative principles

- Implementations MUST store only fields needed for security and audit outcomes.
- Implementations MUST avoid raw identifiers where a hash is sufficient.
- Implementations MUST NOT store raw PII in operational logs.

## Allowed stored/logged fields

Allowed audit fields:

- `timestampBucket` (rounded to 5-minute buckets)
- `requestId` (ephemeral request correlation ID)
- `verifierHash` (rotated salted SHA-256)
- `verdict` (`ALLOW` / `DENY` / `PROMPT`)
- `reasonCode` (from `DenyReasonCode` only)
- `protocolVersion`
- `capabilityProfile`
- Tier-2 accountability fields from ADR-011 / Audit Export Schema v1.1:
  `legalBasis`, `purposeCode`, `dataCategories` (claim names only),
  `policyHash`, `retentionUntil`, `prevRecordHash`, `recordHash`

Forbidden in operational logs:

- Raw subject DID
- Name
- Birthdate / age-date inputs
- Email
- Raw verifier DID

## Anti-correlation rules

- No stable correlators across relying parties: verifier identifiers MUST be salted hashes.
- Salt rotation SHOULD be periodic (e.g., monthly per deployment profile).
- Timestamps MUST be bucketed to 5-minute granularity.
- Cross-RP joins using stable IDs MUST NOT be possible from logs.
- `purposeCode` and `dataCategories` MUST be code tokens, not free text or
  raw values.

## Audience split for reason codes

For DENY reasons, `src/packages/policy-engine/src/deny-reason-codes.ts` is canonical.

- **User audience:** actionable but privacy-preserving explanation.
- **Verifier audience:** bucketed anti-oracle message only.
- **Audit audience:** full technical reason.

Anti-oracle guidance: verifier-facing text MUST NOT allow rule probing via detailed error differences.

## Retention defaults

- Bucketed operational decision logs: 30 days default TTL.
- Aggregated non-user-specific metrics: 90 days default TTL.
- Exported compliance audit bundles: policy-defined; SHOULD be immutable once exported.

## User controls

User MUST be able to:

- Export wallet-held credentials and local decision history.
- Delete locally stored credentials.
- Reset local state (including revocation/status caches and nonce caches).

## Verification steps

Automated checks are implemented in policy-engine tests:

- no raw PII in serialized audit record
- forbidden fields absent from schema
- timestamp bucket enforcement

Manual verification:

- `// TODO(manual-verify):` Confirm downstream log sinks preserve schema without adding raw request payloads.

14:**Conclusion**: Based on the current guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and the technological neutrality principle of the GDPR, the destruction of the decryption key (`K_trans`) while retaining the encrypted audit artifacts constitutes valid erasure, provided that the key is compromised of sufficient entropy and destroyed irreversibly.
20:2.  **Encryption of PII**: All personal data generated during the session is encrypted with `K_trans` before being written to the immutable audit log.
22:4.  **Residual Data**: The encrypted ciphertext remains in the log but is mathematically indistinguishable from random noise without the key.
27:The GDPR does not mandate physical destruction (e.g., degaussing). Recital 26 states that data which has been rendered anonymous is no longer personal data. The Article 29 Working Party (now EDPB) has recognized that "putting data beyond use" can adhere to Art. 17 compliance.
30:Encryption is explicitly mentioned in Art. 32(1)(a) as an appropriate technical measure. When the decryption key is destroyed:
32:*   **Data Minimization (Art. 5(1)(c))**: This method allows for verifiable compliance (the log exists) without retaining the liability (the PII is gone).
35:*   **EDPB Guidelines 04/2020**: Acknowledges that split-key encryption and key destruction can effectively anonymize data.
41:*   **Quantum Threat**: Future quantum computers might break current encryption. *Mitigation: Use quantum-resistant algorithms or ensure data retention policies do not exceed the cryptographic horizon.*
42:*   **Key Leakage**: If `K_trans` is logged or leaked before destruction, the erasure is void. *Mitigation: Strong memory protection (enclaves) and code audits.*

## Finding and scope

Parent: #142 Wave 4 / SEC-AUDIT-4. Preserve the delivered #81 Tier-2 audit-export schema; do not create a duplicate schema design epic.

`audit-export-schema.ts` and `audit-metadata.ts` contain schema/PII/bucketing helpers and tests. The checked app/audit call sites use generic `AuditLog.append(subjectId, metadata)`; no active invocation of `validateNoPii`, `createAuditRecord` or `createAuditExportBundle` was found at those sinks. A `retentionUntil` field is not an executed erasure policy. The detailed local user history is a different purpose from external exports/operational telemetry.

Sources: [schema](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/blob/cacbc95e5ef884e59c688aea41081f8fb7f12fa6/src/packages/policy-engine/src/audit-export-schema.ts), [AuditLog](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/blob/cacbc95e5ef884e59c688aea41081f8fb7f12fa6/src/packages/audit-log/src/index.ts), [metadata budget](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/blob/cacbc95e5ef884e59c688aea41081f8fb7f12fa6/docs/ops/METADATA_BUDGET_V1.md), [two-tier contract](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/blob/cacbc95e5ef884e59c688aea41081f8fb7f12fa6/docs/ops/AUDIT_EXPORT_SCHEMA_V1.md). Current schema helper tests remain evidence for helper behavior. Missing calls in inspected paths do not establish an actual external leak, and do not negate the separate tested consent receipt-export path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Inventory the actual local-history, RP-business, operational and export outputs of the selected application/deployment; record which exist, which are planned and which are out of scope. Identify backups only where the deployment has them.
- [ ] Wire the existing Tier-2 schema into identified Tier-2 external exports. Apply the metadata budget/appropriate schema to identified operational telemetry; the different audiences need not share one format. Check additional properties and profile vocabularies.
- [ ] Test synthetic PII/credential/holder-ID canaries at every relevant output and error path; do not infer anonymity from salted hashes alone.
- [ ] Specify the applicable retention and rotation contracts for identified outputs; implement and test them where required. Test backup cleanup only for actual in-scope backups.
- [ ] Link the existing F-19 durability disposition to affected output consumers; do not duplicate unrelated storage hardening in this issue.
- [ ] Preserve user-controlled detailed Tier-1 history; do not silently apply the external schema to all local data.

This issue does not certify legal compliance or establish lawful retention periods; deployment-specific review remains a gate.

## Evidence discipline

Observed on 2026-10-14 at executable baseline `cacbc95e5ef884e59c688aea41081f8fb7f12fa6`; master/head was re-checked before intake and remained unchanged. Evidence is scoped to the recorded path/profile: reproduced counterexamples, static integration observations and system boundaries have different meanings. None proves that a fix is implemented. [Published finding register](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/blob/6bc484186a6564f89404b44979c679d6feafc15f/docs/security/REPO_EVIDENCE_STATUS_2026-10-14.md) and [dated reproducible probes](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/blob/6bc484186a6564f89404b44979c679d6feafc15f/docs/qa/PCC_LEARNINGS_REPO_AUDIT_2026-10-14.md) were merged through #174 at `624cf9af919fe58a7cba34a05b316b17e49c7e0f`; the linked dated evidence remains unchanged. No production deployment, full browser E2E, official-wallet interoperability, or external assurance is established. Close only with the fix commit, exact-profile negative/integration tests, and dated artifacts.

## Claim-specific evidence maintenance

Documentation-only edits do not require a whole-repository audit. Preserve original test dates/outcomes and code references. Revalidate the affected path/profile when implementation, relevant dependencies/configuration or requirements change. Broad release claims require broader release checks; missing independent evidence does not negate component implementation.


## Retained complete-history goal — 2026-10-15

The goal remains a complete, user-inspectable record of every wallet transaction. The finding about incomplete integration must not reduce that goal to a partial log.

### Befund aus dem Code: Was steht im Audit-Log? (Risiko 4)

Weder das Rechtsmemo noch das Metadata Budget beschreiben, was das Wallet heute ins Audit-Log schreibt. Geprüft am Code-Stand `f4c0073` (master, 2026-10-25) in `WalletService.ts` und `packages/audit-log`.

| Frage | Rechtsmemo | Metadata Budget | Code heute |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Verschlüsselung der Einträge | alle personenbezogenen Daten mit `K_trans` verschlüsselt | – | keine, Einträge im Klartext; `K_trans` gibt es im Code nicht |
| Verifier-Kennung | – | gesalzener Hash | Roh-DID (`verifier_did`, `verifier_id`) |
| Zeitstempel | – | 5-Minuten-Blöcke | volle Zeit, millisekundengenau |
| Claim-Werte | verschlüsselt | verboten | nicht geloggt, nur Claim-Namen (angefragt, geteilt, abgelehnt) |
| Weitere Felder | – | feste Liste | Aussteller-DID, Endpunkt-URLs, signierte Tokens von Lösch- und Meldeanfragen, Freitext-Beschreibung beim Dokument-Signieren |
| Speicherort | unveränderliches Log | – | nur im Arbeitsspeicher des Wallets, keine IndexedDB, kein Escrow aktiv; Export über `exportReport` |
| Aufbewahrung | – | 30 Tage | keine Frist umgesetzt; das inaktive Escrow-Backup hätte 7 Jahre als Voreinstellung |

Das ist der lokale, nutzerkontrollierte Verlauf (Tier 1). Klartext-Verifier-DIDs können dort gewollt sein, damit die Person sieht, wem sie was gezeigt hat. Das Metadata Budget gilt für Betriebs-Logs und Exporte; die dafür gebauten Helfer (`createAuditRecord`, Tier-2-Schema) ruft kein Code auf. Das verfolgt Issue #172.

Folgen für diese DPIA:

1. Risiko 4 ist geklärt: Das Rechtsmemo beschreibt einen Mechanismus, den es im Code nicht gibt. Der Sitzungsschlüssel verschlüsselt die Präsentation, nicht das Log. Eine Löschwirkung durch Crypto-Shredding lässt sich für das Audit-Log nicht behaupten (DP-05).
2. Risiko 3 wird konkret: Verifier-DID, genaue Zeit und Claim-Namen sind verknüpfbar, auf dem Gerät und in jedem Export.
3. Zu entscheiden: ob signierte Tokens von Lösch- und Meldeanfragen und Freitext überhaupt ins Log gehören.
4. Zweck-Codes: Das Schema prüft nur die Form eines Code-Tokens. Eine Liste zulässiger Zweck-Codes gibt es nicht.

7. Conclusion

This Data Protection Impact Assessment confirms that AskMI's identity verification processing is compliant with GDPR Articles 5, 6, 7, 13, 15, 17, 20, 25, 30, 32, and 35.

The processing is necessary (legal requirements for identity verification), proportionate (only boolean predicates, not raw identity data), and safeguarded (crypto-shredding, selective disclosure, tamper-evident audit, metadata minimization).

Residual risks are low after mitigation. The architecture provides strong technical guarantees for the right to erasure (Art. 17): crypto-shredding produces cryptographic proof that the decryption key was destroyed on the AskMI side, rendering AskMI-held ciphertext permanently unrecoverable — rather than relying on deletion promises. This attests to wallet-/AskMI-side erasure and to minimization of what a verifier receives; it does not attest to what a relying party does with data disclosed to it out-of-band.

User-Sovereign Identity & Authorization Infrastructure

input.command:
gh pr comment 150 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Review (2026-10-25, against master `f4c0073`): the direction is right — `signData` should not borrow the audit key — but this can't land as is.

1. **Hardware mode produces an unverifiable token.** `IdentityKeyGuardian.signIdentityPayload` → `WebAuthnService.signWithIdentityKey` returns only `response.signature`. A WebAuthn assertion signs `authenticatorData || SHA-256(clientDataJSON)`, not the payload, and the token drops both, so no recipient can verify it. The header still says `alg: ES256-PoC`.
2. **Encoding is unlabelled.** Software mode yields hex, hardware mode base64; the token doesn't say which.
3. **Signing can now throw** `HARDWARE_IDENTITY_REQUIRED` when WebAuthn exists but no identity key is registered. Erasure and report requests (`requestErasure` / `reportVerifier`) call `signData`, so they would fail closed. That may be correct, but it needs a test and a user-facing message.
4. Commit is unsigned; `master` requires signed commits.

Suggested next step: carry `authenticatorData` + `clientDataJSON` in the token (or define a WebAuthn-specific token type), label the encoding, and add a verification test for both modes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

Existing component evidence remains authoritative for its stated scope. A newer counterexample qualifies only an overlapping claim/path/profile; it does not invalidate unrelated passed tests or completed work.
Keep original QA run dates/SHAs and outcomes immutable. Attach later findings in a separate record or navigation entry.
Close a technical issue only with fix commit and profile-specific negatives/integration evidence; close market gates only with auditable counts/artifacts.

For each reviewed claim, link the component/path, profile/configuration, source revision, verification date, test/observation and known limits. A source SHA records where the observation was made; it does not require a fresh whole-repository audit whenever prose changes. Recheck affected claims when their implementation, relevant dependencies/configuration or profile changes. Unchanged evidence retains its original date and scope. Broad release/deployment claims require broader integration/release checks.

Distinguish reproduced defects, integration gaps, externally unvalidated assurances, deliberate system boundaries and planned functions. Missing evidence is not proof of a malfunction. A component implementation is not automatically an integrated application guarantee.

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

content.text:
I've improved the wallet design and opened it as PR #210: https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/pull/210. I haven't merged it so you can look first.

It keeps the #129 layout and fixes what I found by looking at it in a browser at desktop and phone widths:

- **Trust badge was misleading.** Every card said "✓ Trusted", even a self-issued credential. It now says "Trusted issuer" only when the issuer and credential type are on the wallet's trust list and the entry hasn't expired. Otherwise it says "Not in trust list". In the demo, two of the six cards now show "Not in trust list".
- **The selected tab was never highlighted.** Another CSS rule always won. It's now a solid blue pill.
- **Tab text was the wrong size and weight** because of a CSS ordering mistake.
- **On a phone the tab labels overlapped.** The tab bar now scrolls sideways and the chosen tab slides into view.
- **Buttons used Arial** instead of the app's font.
- **The Requests and Audit pages were narrower than the rest,** and Requests sat off to the left. They now line up with the other pages.
- **On each card, Delete stays quiet until you hover over it,** and the Refresh button is readable on the light background.

All 218 wallet tests pass, including 8 new ones written before the trust-badge code. The type check and lint are clean.

The local wallet is still running at http://localhost:5190/?demo=wallet if you want to click through it. Two things I left out of this PR:
- The audit log shows each startup line twice.
- A few German phrases appear in the English screens.

Separately, the check on PR #153 that was stopped for low memory hasn't been restarted yet.

Comparing with the pre-#129 wallet turned up four more problems. I fixed them and pushed them to the same PR, #210: https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/pull/210. It's still not merged.

No features were lost in #129. Everything from the old version is still there; some of it just moved to the Tools page. What had gone wrong:

- **The Trace page showed the wrong numbers.** #129 renamed the steps to "Requested / Allowed / Sent" but left the old values under them, so "Requested" showed the verdict and "Sent" showed "Request loaded". They now show what each label says. After the age check: 1 item requested, ALLOW, 1 proof and 0 raw values sent. Withheld fields are counted too when there are any.
- **The guided demo was hidden.** The old version opened a walkthrough on the first visit; after #129 it was only reachable from Tools. The Requests page now has a "▶ Guided demo" button. I didn't bring back the automatic pop-up, because in the old version it covered the cards.
- **The data-flow lines ran together** ("offengelegtDaten vergessen nach…") because those styles were missing entirely. They're now a tidy checklist.
- **The Renderer page was white text on white,** so you only saw icons. It's readable now.

All 225 wallet tests pass, including 7 new ones written before the code. The type check is clean.

These need your decision rather than a fix from me:

1. **Too many tabs.** There are 10, and Renderer is labelled "Legacy" for a feature the code describes as not wired into the wallet yet. I'd move Renderer, Proximity and Documents under Tools to get down to about 6.
2. **Dark landing page, light wallet.** The old wallet was dark like the landing page; now "Open demo" jumps from dark mint to light blue, which feels like two different products.
3. **Sovereignty page:** it's a dark pop-up-style box with a close "×", sitting inside a light page.
4. **Mixed languages:** the data-flow and Trace text is German while the rest of the wallet is English.
5. **Small things:** the audit log shows each startup line twice, and Documents and Proximity show their heading twice.

Should I do the tab cleanup (1) next?
explain that tab clean up to me before doing it

Here's the tab cleanup plan. I haven't changed anything yet.

**Why:** the wallet has 10 tabs. On a phone that means 6 or 7 are hidden off the edge of the screen. Several of them are side demos rather than everyday wallet tasks, so the important ones get lost.

**Today's 10 tabs and what each one is:**

| Tab | What it is | Proposal |
|---|---|---|
| Credentials | your cards | keep |
| Requests | someone asks you for proof | keep |
| Trace | what was asked, allowed and sent | keep |
| Sovereignty | totals of data minimised and requests blocked | keep |
| Audit | the raw log | keep, or fold into Trace (your call) |
| Settings | trust list, blocking rules, reset | keep |
| Tools | developer buttons, test credentials | keep, and it gains sections |
| Documents | sign a file on your device | move into Tools |
| Renderer | "Legacy" card previews, a parked feature | move into Tools |
| Proximity | in-person (offline) mDL check | move to Requests as an "In person" card |

**Result:** 7 tabs, or 6 if Audit goes into Trace:

```
Before: Credentials · Requests · Trace · Sovereignty · Documents · Proximity · Renderer · Audit · Settings · Tools
After:  Credentials · Requests · Trace · Sovereignty · Audit · Settings · Tools
```

**What stays the same:**
- Nothing is deleted. Every feature is still one or two clicks away.
- Pages aren't separate web addresses, so no links or bookmarks break.

**What changes for you:**
- Documents and Renderer become labelled sections inside Tools.
- Proximity is no longer a tab. The Requests page gets a fifth card, "In person (ISO 18013-5)", which starts the same offline flow. It's really just another kind of request, and that keeps it visible for demos instead of burying it in Tools.
- A few existing tests that open those tabs get updated. I'd also add new tests for the new routes first.

**Two choices for you:**
1. **Audit:** keep it as its own tab (7 tabs), or put the log at the bottom of Trace (6 tabs)? I'd keep it separate: Trace is the readable story and Audit is the raw evidence, and people look for them for different reasons.
2. **Proximity:** a card on Requests (my recommendation) or a section in Tools?

Tell me your picks, or say "go with your recommendations", and I'll build it into PR #210.

Moving it into a card costs almost nothing — the actual flow lives in ProximityView, not the tab.

My picks:

    Audit: keep it as its own tab. I agree with your reasoning — Trace is the interpreted story, Audit is the raw append-only log. Different audiences (user vs. auditor/debugging), and per the project's own principles the audit trail should stay separately visible, not demoted to a footer under a derived view. Also, App.tsx:1829 already gates ['requests', 'trace', 'audit'] together in one condition — folding Audit into Trace would complicate that grouping for no gain. Result: 7 tabs.

    Proximity: card on Requests. Agreed, it's just another request type (in-person, ISO 18013-5). Keeping it as a top-level tab overstates a mock flow; burying it in Tools would hurt demo visibility. A fifth card on Requests is the right balance.

Additional review notes on the plan itself:

    The tab list is a single array, so the nav cut is trivial. Keep the aria-current="page" pattern intact and make sure the Tools-internal sections (Documents, Renderer) get their own headings/anchors so deep links still land somewhere sensible.
    showProximityPreview and ProximityView are mounted at App level, not inside the Proximity page — moving the tab should not require touching that modal wiring, only where the launch button lives.

**The first approach broke the workflow file.** `fdcfc73` put `continue-on-error: true` on the `review` job. I'll trace where the startup audit lines are emitted and check whether the app runs under React StrictMode (double-invoked effects in dev) or the wallet is actually started twice.
The sandbox checkout has no installed dependencies, so I can't run the runtime probe here. But the static analysis is conclusive on its own. Let me do one final check on the `loadWalletCredentials` path to make sure it isn't also logging on init.
**Verdict: the doubled startup lines are a dev-mode StrictMode artifact — but the effect is not idempotent, so there's a small real fix worth making.**

**Root cause chain:**

1. `main.tsx:7` mounts `<App />` inside `<React.StrictMode>`. In development builds, StrictMode intentionally mounts components, runs effects, unmounts, and re-runs effects once to surface missing cleanup.
2. The bootstrap effect at `App.tsx:356–398` has an empty dependency array and **no cleanup function**: it calls `init()` unconditionally at the end (`App.tsx:397`). So in dev the whole sequence — `🔓 Initializing Wallet Service...` → `🔑 Wallet Decrypted & Ready` → passkey status line → credential load — runs twice, and each `addLog` call appends (`App.tsx:256`, `setLogs(prev => [...prev, ...])`). Hence every startup line appears twice.
3. In a **production build, StrictMode's double-invocation does not occur**, so users never see this. It's dev-only as a *visual* symptom.

**Why it's not entirely benign:**

The effect has real side effects beyond logging: `walletRef.current.initialize('123456')` and the WebAuthn availability/identity checks (`App.tsx:358–387`) run twice in dev. The log doubling is the *visible* evidence that the bootstrap isn't idempotent. On the first (discarded) StrictMode pass, `initialize()` decrypts the vault and the async passkey checks fire — the second pass then re-initializes an already-initialized wallet. If `WalletService.initialize()` isn't safe to call twice, the duplicate could mask or cause state races. That's worth checking in `WalletService.ts` even though the symptom is cosmetic.

**Recommendation:**

- Don't remove StrictMode — it's doing its job by exposing this.
- Make the bootstrap a proper effect: either return a cancellation guard (a `let cancelled = false` set in the cleanup, checked before each `addLog`/`setStatus`), or guard with a `useRef` "already bootstrapped" flag so the second StrictMode pass is a no-op. The ref-guard is the smaller change and fits the existing `bootstrapRef` pattern at `App.tsx:353`.
- Keep the explicit-reset path working: `handleResetWallet` re-runs `bootstrapRef.current`, so the guard must be resettable there (e.g. the reset clears the flag before re-invoking bootstrap).
- Add a regression test asserting the startup sequence appears exactly once per mount — in the test environment, `render(<App />)` from `App.test.tsx` doesn't go through `main.tsx`, so the double-mount doesn't reproduce there today; the test should mount inside StrictMode to actually cover it.

One caveat, honestly stated: I couldn't run the runtime probe in this sandbox (the checkout has no `node_modules` installed), so the StrictMode explanation is static analysis of `main.tsx`, the bootstrap effect, and `addLog` — it fits the symptom exactly (each startup line doubled, nothing else doubled), but the confirming browser/test run should happen in your environment. If you want, I can write the guard + regression test as a PR next.

I have enough for a plan. Here's what #150 really involves, in three layers, before I build anything.

**What's wrong today:**
1. **The wallet never saves the passkey's public key.** At registration it stores a placeholder with empty fields (`webauthn.ts:255`, commented "for this PoC"). Without that key, no hardware signature can ever be verified, by the wallet or anyone else.
2. **Hardware signing throws away what's needed to verify it.** A passkey signs `authenticatorData + hash(clientDataJSON)`, not the data itself, and the code keeps only the bare signature.
3. **Two places rely on these signatures:**
   - **Proof tokens** for erasure and report requests (#150's change): the hardware version can't be verified, and the token doesn't say which encoding it uses.
   - **Decision records on `master` today:** in hardware mode the check only looks at the labels and then logs "✅ Bound to Hardware Identity Key". Nothing is verified. A QA note from 2026-07-12 lists this as a known limitation, but there's no issue for it and the log line overstates what's checked.

**Proposed plan, as 3 PRs in order:**

| PR | What | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Signing support (shared-crypto):** save the passkey's real public key at registration; add a new signing function that returns the full passkey response; add a verify helper that checks challenge, type, site, user-verification flag and signature. Only new functions, nothing existing changes. | Low |
| 2 | **Proof tokens (replaces #150):** sign with the identity key; labelled format (key type, encoding) with the passkey data included; tests that verify both modes. Erasure/report show a clear "register your passkey first" message instead of failing silently. | Medium |
| 3 | **Decision records:** actually verify hardware signatures and fix the "✅" log line. This adds fields to the decision-record format (`shared-types`), which counts as a public API change. | Needs your OK |

**Three decisions for you:**
1. **Decision-record format change (PR 3):** CLAUDE.md requires your explicit approval for public API changes. OK to add the passkey data fields to the decision record?
2. **Devices already registered without a public key:** their hardware signatures can never be verified. I'd recommend marking them "unverified" and asking the user once to re-register the passkey, never accepting them silently. The alternative is forcing re-registration straight away.
3. **What to do with #150:** it's an auto-generated Jules branch with an unsigned commit, so it can't merge as is. I'd close it and replace it with my own signed PR that credits it, as we did with #167 → #201.

I'd also open an issue for the decision-record gap, so it's tracked rather than only noted in a QA document.

Tell me your answers, or "go with your recommendations". I'd start with PR 1 either way, since it changes no existing behaviour.

The three decisions

1. Decision-record format change (PR 3): OK, approved — with one constraint.
Add the passkey data fields (public key ref, authenticatorData, clientDataJSON/hash, UV flag, signature encoding) as additive, optional fields. Old records without those fields must remain readable and must be treated by the new verify path as unverified, not as errors. That keeps it a backward-compatible change rather than a breaking API change, and it dovetails with decision 2. Also fix the log line in the same PR — "✅ Bound to Hardware Identity Key" must not print unless a signature actually verified. A log line that overstates what was checked is worse than no line, because it's the thing users and auditors will trust.

2. Already-registered devices: mark unverified + one-time re-register prompt. Do not silently accept, and do not hard-block.
Their recommendation is right. Reasons: silently accepting preserves the exact gap we're fixing (records that claim hardware binding without verifiability); an immediate forced re-registration breaks every existing device for a PoC-era gap and violates "the passkey IS the account" continuity (App.tsx's Model A comment). The one-time prompt mirrors the existing first-run pattern — no surprise biometric ceremony, the user gets framing before navigator.credentials.create() fires. The unverified state must be visible in Trace/Audit, not just internal.

3. Close #150, replace with a signed PR that credits it: yes.
Consistent with the #167 → #201 precedent, and an unsigned auto-generated Jules commit can't merge anyway. Credit in the PR body, close #150 with a comment pointing at the replacement so the history is traceable.

And yes to the tracking issue — a known verification gap that only lives in a QA document from 2026-07-12 is exactly the kind of thing that gets rediscovered twice. One issue, referencing the QA note, closed by PR 3.

So: go — start PR 1. Its risk profile (new functions only, no behavior change) makes it the right first step regardless of the answers above.
The "insight before login" idea

The idea itself is good and squarely on-mission — but only in one direction, with guardrails.

Why it's on-mission: miTch's whole premise is that data about people already exists and the value is in making it nachvollziehbar — visible and controllable. The same logic applies to the verifier: before the user presents anything, the wallet should say what it already knows about who's asking. That's not new surveillance; it's surfacing existing knowledge. It also fits the "honest trust badge" work from #210 — you've already started down this road.

The one direction that's fine: show the wallet user what's already known about the verifier — from data miTch already holds locally: origin/redirect URI, whether the verifier is on the trust list, prior request history from Trace (what they asked before, what was actually sent), whether a request deviates from their previous pattern ("this site has never asked for your address before"). Edge-first, local-only, no new collection. This is verifier transparency and it strengthens consent quality.

The direction that's not fine: anything that probes the requesting party to generate that insight — fingerprinting the verifier's device, active lookups keyed on the request, or third-party reputation queries that leak "user X is about to interact with verifier Y" before consent. That would make miTch the thing it exists to prevent. So: passive, already-collected signals only, and label every inference as inference ("based on 3 past requests"), not fact.

"Start with the device": if that means showing the user what their own device reveals pre-login (user agent, origin, session signals) — fine as a transparency display, but it must not be used as an input for silent decisions, and it must not become a fingerprinting surface itself.

Concrete suggestion: keep this out of the current three-PR passkey work entirely — it's a different concern (presentation-layer transparency vs. signature verification). Track it as its own issue/ADR sketch, and design it against the Trace and Requests surfaces you just restructured in #213, since the "In person" card and Trace are the natural places this insight would live. If you want, after PR 1 lands I can outline what a "verifier insight before consent" panel would and wouldn't show, as a design note rather than code.

## Your idea: show people what's already visible about them before they log in

I think it's a good idea, and it fits miTch well, with a few rules. One clarification first: the reply you pasted mostly read it as showing the user what's known about the *verifier*. Your wording reads to me as the other direction: someone arrives at login, and *before* they log in, we show them what any website can already see about them and their device. The honest message is "this is what's out there about you, and we didn't even have to ask."

**Why it's good:**
- It makes the problem miTch solves tangible in about five seconds. Seeing "your screen size, your time zone, your fonts, your GPU" lands harder than any explanation of data minimisation.
- It's a strong demo opening, and useful for the G1 interviews too: show what's visible first, then show how little the wallet hands over.
- It's honest. You're not inventing a threat; you're showing what every site already gets.

**Rules, or it turns into the thing miTch is against:**
1. **Everything happens on the device.** Compute the signals in the browser, show them, then discard them. Never send, store or log them, not even in our own audit log.
2. **Never use them for decisions.** No risk score, no "suspicious device" check, no blocking. As soon as it feeds a decision, it's fingerprinting.
3. **No server lookups.** The IP address and the location derived from it would need a server to echo them back, so I'd leave them out. Alternatively, say plainly that every server you contact sees them, without fetching them.
4. **Say what each item means,** for example "your time zone narrows you down to a region". Mark estimates as estimates; a combined "uniqueness" figure, for instance, is a guess.
5. **The person can close it,** and it doesn't come back on every login.

**Where it would live:** the welcome and locked screens of the wallet, and possibly the landing page. It doesn't belong in the passkey work, so I'd track it as its own issue with a short design note first.

So yes, I like it. The other direction from the pasted reply, showing what's known about the verifier from our own past interactions, is also good and can sit in the same design note.

## Passkey work: starting PR 1

Your decisions are recorded: the decision-record fields are optional and old records count as "unverified"; already-registered devices are marked unverified with a one-time prompt to re-register; #150 gets closed and credited; and there will be a tracking issue. Starting PR 1 now: signing support only, with no change to existing behaviour.

## Finding (2026-10-25, master 07ceb5f)
In `WalletService` (`src/apps/wallet-pwa/src/services/WalletService.ts`, capsule check around line 1010), a decision capsule whose `wallet_attestation_protection` is `HARDWARE_BOUND` is **not signature-checked**. The code only checks that `wallet_attestation_method === 'webauthn'` and `wallet_attestation_encoding === 'base64'`, then logs:

> ✅ Capsule Attestation Bound to Hardware Identity Key (WebAuthn)

The software path does verify (ECDSA against the software key).

Why it can't be verified today:
1. `WebAuthnService.signWithIdentityKey` returns only `response.signature`. A WebAuthn assertion signs `authenticatorData || SHA-256(clientDataJSON)`, and both are discarded.
2. Registration stores a placeholder public key (`x: '', y: ''`), so there is no key to verify against.

Effect: when a hardware passkey is registered, a capsule with the right metadata labels passes the check, and the log line overstates what was checked.

Previously noted as a residual gap in `docs/qa/WEBAUTHN_FAIL_CLOSED_2026-07-12.md` ("WebAuthn assertion verification"), but not tracked as an issue.

## Plan (agreed 2026-10-25)
1. **PR 1** (shared-crypto): store the real P-256 public key at registration, add `signWithIdentityKeyAssertion` (full assertion) and `verifyIdentityAssertion`. New functions only.
2. **PR 2**: proof tokens for erasure/report (replaces #150), using the identity key with a labelled, verifiable format.
3. **PR 3**: capsule attestation carries the assertion parts as **optional, additive** fields. Old capsules without them are treated as **unverified** (not errors). The "✅ Bound" line is only logged after a signature actually verifies, and the unverified state is visible in Trace/Audit.

Already-registered devices (placeholder key): mark as unverified and show a one-time, framed prompt to re-register the passkey. Don't silently accept, and don't hard-block.

Closed by PR 3.

PR 1 of 3 for #218 (and the replacement for #150's approach). **New functions only; no existing behaviour changes.**

## Why
A passkey doesn't sign the caller's data. It signs `authenticatorData || SHA-256(clientDataJSON)`. Today the wallet keeps only the bare signature and stores a placeholder public key (`x: '', y: ''`), so no hardware identity signature can be verified (see #218).

## What's added (`@askmi/shared-crypto`)
- **Registration keeps the real key.** `registerIdentityKey` converts the registration SPKI to a P-256 JWK. RS256 or no exposed key gives `null`, so those signatures stay unverifiable and nothing is guessed.
- **`WebAuthnService.signWithIdentityKeyAssertion(data)`**: challenge = SHA-256(data); returns `{ version, credentialId, rpId, authenticatorData, clientDataJSON, signature }` (base64url, DER signature). It never falls back to a software key and throws `IDENTITY_KEY_NOT_REGISTERED` instead.
- **`WebAuthnService.getIdentityPublicKeyJwk()`**: returns the stored key, or `null` for no key or a legacy placeholder registration.
- **`verifyIdentityAssertion({ data, assertion, publicKeyJwk, expectedRpId, expectedOrigin? })`** checks:
  - client data `type` is `webauthn.get`
  - the challenge equals SHA-256(data)
  - the origin matches, if one is given
  - the rpId hash matches
  - the UP and UV flags are set
  - the ECDSA signature is valid (DER converted to P1363)

  It never throws. It returns `{ valid: true }` or `{ valid: false, reason }` with one of `NO_PUBLIC_KEY`, `MALFORMED`, `WRONG_TYPE`, `CHALLENGE_MISMATCH`, `ORIGIN_MISMATCH`, `RP_ID_MISMATCH`, `USER_NOT_PRESENT`, `USER_NOT_VERIFIED`, `BAD_SIGNATURE`.
- **Exports:** only the verification API is exported from the package index; the base64 helpers stay internal.
- **Unchanged:** `signWithIdentityKey` (bare signature) is untouched for its existing callers. PR 2 and PR 3 move them over.

## Tests (written first)
They use a simulated platform authenticator: a real P-256 key that answers `navigator.credentials.create/get` like a browser passkey, with DER signatures.
- **Verifier, 17 tests:**
  - a genuine assertion verifies
  - each failure reason is triggered on its own: wrong data, wrong rpId, UV missing, UP missing, wrong type, wrong origin, tampered authenticatorData, a different key, the placeholder key, and garbage input (reported as MALFORMED, no throw)
  - 25 genuine assertions in a row verify (DER integers with and without leading zeros)
  - DER→P1363 edge cases
  - SPKI→JWK conversion
- **Service, 7 tests (fake-indexeddb):**
  - registration stores the real key; stores none when the authenticator exposes none
  - a legacy placeholder registration gives `null`
  - signer → verifier works end to end
  - the challenge is SHA-256 even for short data
  - the signer refuses without a passkey, even where WebAuthn is unavailable
  - the legacy bare signer is unchanged

`fake-indexeddb@^6.2.5` is added as a shared-crypto devDependency; it's the same version secure-storage and phase0-security already use (lockfile +3 lines).

PR 2 replaces #150 (identity-key proof tokens). PR 3 adds the optional capsule fields, real verification and an honest log line, and closes #218.

## Idea (2026-10-25)
Before someone logs in to the wallet, show them what any website can already see about them and their device, without being asked. It makes the problem miTch solves concrete in seconds and works as the demo's opening act.

[miTch-Transparency-Layer](https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch-Transparency-Layer) (MV3 Chrome extension) already does the general version per site. ## Guardrails (agreed)
1. **On-device only.** Compute in the browser, show, discard. Never sent, stored or logged, including our own audit log.
2. **Never an input to decisions.** No risk score, no "suspicious device", no blocking. Otherwise it becomes fingerprinting.
3. **No server lookups.** No IP or geo echo. If mentioned at all, say plainly that every server you contact sees your IP.
4. **Label every item** by layer (observed / potential / unknown) and say what it reveals.
5. **Dismissible,** not shown on every login.

## Placement
Wallet welcome / locked screens (possibly the landing page). The companion direction, "what we already know about this *verifier* from our own past interactions", fits the Requests/Trace surfaces from #213 and can share the same note.

Design note first (`docs/...`), then a small PR. Starts after the passkey track (#218: PR 1 #219, PR 2, PR 3).

PR 2 of 3 for #218. **Replaces #150.** Credit goes to the Jules refactor in #150 for the right direction: `signData` must not borrow the audit key.

## What #150's review asked for, and where it's addressed
| Review point on #150 | This PR |
|---|---|
| Hardware mode produced an unverifiable token (bare signature only) | Hardware tokens carry the full WebAuthn assertion (`signWithIdentityKeyAssertion` from #219) and verify against the passkey public key |
| Encoding unlabelled (hex vs base64) | Header labels `typ`, `v`, `alg`, `key`, `kid`, `enc`; everything is base64url |
| Signing can throw `HARDWARE_IDENTITY_REQUIRED`; erasure/report would fail without explanation | Typed `IdentityKeyRequiredError`. Erasure/report return a clear "set up your passkey" message, send nothing, and record `FAILED / IDENTITY_KEY_REQUIRED` in the audit log. Tested |
| Unsigned commit | Signed commit on a fresh branch |

## Token format v2 (`utils/proof-token.ts`)
`base64url(header) . base64url(payload) . base64url(signature part)`. The signature covers **`header.payload`**; the old format signed only the payload.
- `key: hardware-passkey`, `alg: webauthn-es256`: the signature part is the assertion JSON, checked with `verifyIdentityAssertion` (needs the passkey public key and the expected rpId).
- `key: software-session`, `alg: ES256`: a raw P-256 signature from the wallet's software identity key, used **only where WebAuthn is unavailable** (Node, tests, old browsers). Only the session public key can check it.
- `verifyProofToken` never throws. It rejects the old unlabelled format (`UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT`) and garbage (`MALFORMED`).

No code in the repo reads these tokens; they're POSTed to verifier/authority endpoints as before. Receivers of the old format would need updating, and there are none in this repo.

## Key choice in `signData`
1. Passkey registered → passkey assertion.
2. WebAuthn available but no passkey → refuse. No silent software downgrade.
3. No WebAuthn → software session key.

The audit key is no longer used for signing requests.

## Tests (written first)
- `proof-token.test.ts` (10):
  - both modes verify, and the header labels are checked
  - tampering is caught: changed payload, changed `kid` (header covered), the wrong passkey
  - missing key and missing rpId are reported
  - the legacy v1 format is rejected, and garbage is reported as MALFORMED
- `WalletService.test.ts` (+4):
  - an erasure token verifies with the session key
  - erasure and report stop when no passkey is registered: nothing is sent, the audit records the reason
  - with a passkey, the full assertion is used (and never the bare signer), over exactly `header.payload`
- The 5 existing fail-closed delivery tests are unchanged and pass.

## Evidence (c30ff31, 2026-10-25, Node 22, Windows)
- wallet-pwa: 19 files, 244/244 tests, exit 0; `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- eslint: no errors. The 4 existing `no-explicit-any` warnings are on lines this PR doesn't touch.
- The new files are Prettier-clean. `WalletService.ts` and `WalletService.test.ts` were already not Prettier-clean on master.

## Not in this PR
- Proof tokens are still stored in the audit log (`proof_token`), as before. Whether they should be dropped belongs to #172 (audit export minimisation).
- PR 3: decision-capsule attestation verification and the honest log line (closes #218).

PR 3 of 3 for #218. Closes #218.

## The gap, shown by the new tests on master
Before this PR, a decision capsule claiming a device-passkey signature was presented even if it had been **changed after signing**, **signed for another site**, or had its **proof stripped**. The check only compared labels and then logged "✅ Capsule Attestation Bound to Hardware Identity Key". The new tests failed on master for exactly these reasons ("promise resolved instead of rejecting").

## What changes
**`shared-types` (additive, approved on the "optional fields" terms):**
- `DecisionCapsule.wallet_attestation_assertion?: WalletAttestationAssertion`, the full WebAuthn assertion. It isn't part of the signed payload.
- `wallet_attestation_encoding` gains `'webauthn-assertion'`.
- The JSON schema gets the optional property. Old capsules stay valid.

**Signing:** with a passkey, the capsule is signed via `signWithIdentityKeyAssertion` (#219) and carries the assertion. The software path is unchanged.

**Verification in `generatePresentation`**, against **this device's registration**, never against the rpId written inside the assertion (new `WebAuthnService.getIdentityVerificationKey()`):

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Registered passkey with stored public key, assertion verifies | `✅ Capsule Attestation Verified (device passkey)` |
| …assertion fails (changed capsule, other site, other key) | **SECURITY ALERT**, nothing is presented |
| Hardware claim, key stored, assertion missing (stripped) | **SECURITY ALERT** |
| Hardware claim, but no passkey registered | **SECURITY ALERT** |
| Legacy passkey registered before #219 (no stored key) | `⚠️ … not verifiable on this device … Re-register the passkey` (warning in the Audit page). **Proceeds; never logged as verified** |
| Software capsule | Unchanged ECDSA check |

**Re-register prompt (decision 2):** a one-time, framed, dismissible prompt on the Credentials page when the passkey has no stored key. "Re-register passkey" stores the real key; "Not now" is remembered in `localStorage` (try/catch, so blocked storage just shows it again). No surprise biometric prompt and no hard block. Note: re-registering creates a new passkey on the device; the old one stays in the OS keychain but is no longer used.

Presentation warnings starting with ⚠️ now show as warnings, not info, in the Audit log.

## Tests (written first)
- **WalletService (+9; the old bare-signature test was rewritten):**
  - the capsule is signed with the full assertion over exactly the payload
  - a genuine capsule verifies and is only then logged as verified
  - blocked: a changed capsule, the wrong rpId, a stripped assertion, a hardware claim without a passkey
  - legacy passkey: unverified, and the flow proceeds; an old capsule without the assertion on a legacy device counts as unverified
  - `passkeyNeedsReRegistration()`
- **App (+3):** the prompt shows and re-registration calls `registerIdentityKey`; "Not now" is remembered across reloads; no prompt for a verifiable passkey.
- **shared-crypto (+3):** `getIdentityVerificationKey` returns the registered rpId and key; null key for a legacy registration; null without a passkey.

## End-to-end check in a real browser (Chrome virtual authenticator, dev server)
1. "Create my AskMI account" registered a real passkey, and a real P-256 public key was stored (rpId `localhost`).
2. Age check: the Audit page shows **"✅ Capsule Attestation Verified (device passkey)"**. Chrome's assertion was verified by `verifyIdentityAssertion`.
3. Stored key replaced with the legacy placeholder, page reloaded: the prompt appears, and the age check logs the **"not verifiable … Re-register"** warning, with no ✅.
4. "Re-register passkey" stored a real key again and the prompt disappeared. The next age check showed **"✅ Capsule Attestation Verified (device passkey)"**.

- shared-crypto, policy-engine, mcp-server test suites: exit 0.

`docs/qa/WEBAUTHN_FAIL_CLOSED_2026-07-12.md` still lists "WebAuthn assertion verification" as a residual gap. It's now closed for the wallet-side capsule check. That doc should get a dated update after reading `docs/DOCS_CANON.md`; I can do that as a docs-only PR.

# WebAuthn Fail-Closed — Finding & Fix (2026-07-12)

**Status:** Increment 1 fixed `webauthn.ts`; Increment 2 wires the real wallet
identity-key gate via `IdentityKeyGuardian`. Branch `fix/webauthn-fail-closed`
off `master`.
**Invariant enforced:** North-Star **Fail-Closed** ("ambiguity = DENY") applied to the
hardware-bound identity key. See also `docs/_core/10_KEY_PROTECTION_REALITY.md`
(arriving via PR #130) for the honest crypto-protection baseline.

## TL;DR
The wallet's "real secure key" is the **WebAuthn/passkey identity key** (platform
authenticator, `userVerification:'required'`, `residentKey:'required'`). A software
ECDSA fallback exists for environments without WebAuthn (Node/tests/legacy browsers).
The problem: that software fallback was reachable **as an error-recovery and
missing-key path even when WebAuthn was available**, and the resulting signature was
**typed identically** to a hardware one — so a caller (or an attacker who can induce an
error) could obtain a software-signed result that silently **bypasses the secure key**.
This contradicts the Fail-Closed invariant.

## The four silent-downgrade surfaces (as found)
| # | Location | Behaviour |
|---|----------|-----------|
| 1 | `wallet-pwa/src/services/WalletService.ts:461-476` | No passkey registered → inline software ECDSA `policyPrivateKey` created and used to sign **all** DecisionCapsules. Only a `console.warn`. |
| 2 | `shared-crypto/src/webauthn.ts` `signWithIdentityKey` | Missing/`software-fallback` meta → `SoftwareFallback.sign()`, returned as a bare signature string. |
| 3 | `shared-crypto/src/webauthn.ts` `provePresenceDetailed` (final `catch`) | **Worst.** Any unexpected assertion error (not `NotAllowed`/`Security`/`InvalidState`/`NotSupported`) → `SoftwareFallback.sign()` **returned as a valid result**, even when WebAuthn is present and a real passkey exists. Fail-**open**. |
| 4 | `shared-crypto/src/webauthn.ts` `verifyPresence` | Verifier side accepts any `attestation.length > 0` — does not distinguish `method:'webauthn'` from `method:'software-fallback'`. |

### Root cause
The protection level is **invisible and unenforced**. `PresenceProof` carries a
`method: 'webauthn' | 'software-fallback'` marker, but `provePresence()` discards it

## What remains after Increment 2
- **Point 4** (`verifyPresence`): make the verifier reject `method:'software-fallback'`
  in production paths. This needs the full proof object, not the legacy bare string.
- **Presence level propagation:** `provePresence()` still returns only `.signature`
  for compatibility; callers that need assurance must use `provePresenceDetailed()`
  and enforce `method:'webauthn'`.
- **WebAuthn assertion verification:** the current wallet-side hardware attestation
  is fail-closed against software downgrade, but it is not a full server-side
  WebAuthn assertion verifier. That belongs in the verifier/native hook work where
  public key, authenticatorData, clientDataJSON, signature counter, rpId and origin
  can be checked together.

These are tracked here rather than fixed silently, to keep the increment small and the
security-critical change reviewable.

# WebAuthn Assertion Verification — Wallet Side (2026-10-25)

**Scope:** wallet-pwa + `@askmi/shared-crypto` + `@askmi/shared-types`, browser wallet profile.
**Follows:** [WEBAUTHN_FAIL_CLOSED_2026-07-12.md](WEBAUTHN_FAIL_CLOSED_2026-07-12.md). That record and
its outcomes stay unchanged. This record addresses only its residual item
"WebAuthn assertion verification", and only on the wallet side.
**Tracking:** #218 (closed by #222).

## Finding (reproduced 2026-10-25 on master `07ceb5f`)
- A decision capsule labelled `HARDWARE_BOUND` was **not signature-checked** in
  `WalletService.generatePresentation`. Only the metadata labels were compared, followed by
  the log line "✅ Capsule Attestation Bound to Hardware Identity Key (WebAuthn)".
- Two causes:
  - `WebAuthnService.signWithIdentityKey` returned only `response.signature`, discarding
    `authenticatorData` and `clientDataJSON`.
  - Registration stored a placeholder public key (`x: ''`, `y: ''`), so there was nothing to
    verify against.
- Reproduced by tests written before the fix. On master, a capsule changed after signing, a
  capsule signed for another rpId, and a capsule with its assertion stripped were all
  presented ("promise resolved instead of rejecting").

## Fix (three PRs)
| PR | Merge commit | Change |
|---|---|---|
| #219 | `faadb28` | Registration stores the real P-256 public key (SPKI → JWK; RS256 or no key → `null`). `signWithIdentityKeyAssertion` returns the full assertion (challenge = SHA-256(data)). `verifyIdentityAssertion` checks type, challenge, optional origin, rpId hash, UP and UV flags, and the ECDSA signature over `authenticatorData ‖ SHA-256(clientDataJSON)`. It never throws. |
| #221 | `87c5ab7` | Proof tokens (erasure, verifier report, document proof) are signed with the identity key, not the audit key. v2 format is labelled and covers its header. A passkey token carries the assertion. WebAuthn available but no passkey → the request is refused with `IDENTITY_KEY_REQUIRED`. Replaces #150. |
| #222 | `4b7e393` | Capsules carry the optional `wallet_attestation_assertion` (additive `shared-types` field, encoding `webauthn-assertion`). They are verified against **this device's registration** (`getIdentityVerificationKey`; never the rpId inside the assertion). There is a one-time prompt to re-register legacy passkeys. |

### Capsule check after #222
| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Stored public key; assertion verifies | `✅ Capsule Attestation Verified (device passkey)` |
| Stored public key; assertion fails (changed capsule, other rpId, other key) | `SECURITY ALERT`, not presented |
| Hardware claim; key stored; assertion missing | `SECURITY ALERT` |
| Hardware claim; no passkey registered | `SECURITY ALERT` |
| Legacy passkey (registered before #219, no stored key) | `⚠️ … not verifiable … Re-register the passkey`. **Proceeds**, never logged as verified (product decision, #218) |
| Software capsule (no WebAuthn) | ECDSA check, unchanged |

## Evidence
- **Unit and integration tests (Node 22, Windows, vitest):**
  - shared-crypto: 28 files, 291/291 at #219 head `ca2108c`. The verifier and service tests use a simulated P-256 platform authenticator with DER signatures.
  - wallet-pwa: 244/244 at #221 head `c30ff31`; 255/255 at #222 head `93c5453`.
  - CI required checks passed on each PR before merge.
- **Real-browser check (2026-10-25, #222 branch, Vite dev server over HTTP on localhost, Chrome via Playwright, CDP virtual authenticator `ctap2`/`internal`, UV on):**
  1. "Create my AskMI account" stored a real P-256 public key (rpId `localhost`).
  2. Age check: the Audit log showed `✅ Capsule Attestation Verified (device passkey)`.
  3. With the stored key replaced by the legacy placeholder and the page reloaded, the re-register prompt was shown and the age check logged the "not verifiable … Re-register" warning, with no ✅.
  4. "Re-register passkey" stored a real key and hid the prompt. The next age check logged `✅ Capsule Attestation Verified (device passkey)`.

## Known limits (still open)
- **Wallet-side only.** This is not a server-side WebAuthn verifier. The signature counter is not checked, and the capsule check does not pass an expected origin (rpId hash and UV are checked).
- **Legacy passkeys** (no stored key) stay unverifiable until re-registered. By decision they proceed with a warning.
- **Stripped-assertion detection** relies on a stored key. On a legacy device, a capsule without an assertion is "unverified", not blocked.
- **RS256 passkeys** get no stored key and are therefore unverifiable.
- **Re-registering creates a new passkey.** The old one stays in the OS keychain but is no longer used.
- **Not addressed here** (from the 2026-07-12 record): point 4 (`verifyPresence` rejecting `software-fallback`) and `provePresence()` presence-level propagation. Presence proofs are still bare signatures.
- **Proof tokens are still stored in the audit log** (`proof_token`). Minimisation belongs to #172.

#223 is merged into `master` (`5e25221`). The re-run passed, so it really was a timing flake.

**Cleanup:** I confirmed #223's docs on `master` match its branch head exactly, then deleted that branch on GitHub and locally. I also removed the old `wt-passkey` worktree folder; it had no uncommitted tracked changes.

**The timeout fix is open as #225:** https://github.com/Late-bloomer420/miTch/pull/225. It's a one-line test change plus a comment, and no product code is touched.
- **What it does:** `describe('SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s', { timeout: 120_000 }, …)`. Only the two SLH-DSA tests get the 120s limit. Every other shared-crypto test keeps 30s, so a test that really hangs still fails fast.
- **Why 120s:** each test takes about 4s locally but took 31.3s on CI, roughly 8× slower. 120s leaves room even on a slow runner.
- **Proof the setting takes effect:** I temporarily set the block limit to 1ms while keeping `--testTimeout 30000` on the command line. Exactly the two SLH-DSA tests failed and the other 23 passed, so the block setting wins over the command line. I set it back to 120s before committing. 25/25 pass with the real value.
- **Formatting:** this test file already fails Prettier's check on `master` (4-space indentation). I left it alone so the diff stays one line; reformatting belongs in a separate style-only PR.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The "128s" in SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s means "small signature". It trades signing speed for size, which is why it's about 300× slower than ML-DSA in the same file (4s against roughly 15ms).
- `git push` printed a GitHub notice saying Dependabot lists 161 known vulnerabilities on `master` (62 high). That's worth keeping in mind for the Vite 6→8 PR, which will move a large part of the dependency tree anyway.

**Merge #225.** All checks green, and the diff is exactly the right shape for a flake fix:

- **+3/−1, one file.** `describe('SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s', { timeout: 120_000 }, …)` — block-scoped, so only the two genuinely slow tests get the headroom; every other shared-crypto test keeps the 30s default and still fails fast if it hangs. That's the correct scope for this fix — a global timeout bump would have masked future hangs.
- **The precedence proof is the part I appreciate most**: temporarily setting the block to 1ms while keeping `--testTimeout 30000` on the CLI, confirming exactly the two SLH-DSA tests (and only those) failed, then restoring 120s. That's empirical verification that the setting actually takes effect in this vitest version, rather than assuming the docs are right — and it mirrors how the config behaves in CI (block override > CLI default).
- **120s is well-reasoned**: 31.3s observed on CI ≈ 8× the local ~4s, so 120s covers even a runner having a worse day than the one that flaked #223. And the comment explains *why* the timeout is high (SLH-DSA's deliberate speed-for-size trade), so nobody "fixes" it back down later without knowing the history.
